title: Berkshire 2004 letter: float, disciplined underwriting, and fractional ownership of businesses
summary: Buffett's 2004 letter covers 21.9% compounded book value growth, how NICO and GEICO turn commodity insurance into float that can cost less than nothing, why he treats stocks as business ownership, and how director fees and unexpensed options distort incentives. He also admits mistakes and warns on the trade deficit.

principles.text: Judge long-term results against a low-cost index fund; otherwise management adds nothing.
principles.quote: Our shareholders can buy the S&P through an index fund at very low cost. Unless we achieve gains in per-share intrinsic value in the future that outdo the S&P, Charlie and I will be adding nothing to what you can accomplish on your own.

principles.text: Float is wonderful only if it doesn't come at a high price; underwriting profit makes it better than free.
principles.quote: Float is wonderful – if it doesn't come at a high price. Its cost is determined by underwriting results, meaning how the expenses and losses we will ultimately pay compare with the premiums we have received.

principles.text: In a commodity business, price for profit and accept shrinking volume rather than match the most optimistic competitor.
principles.quote: But we instead consistently priced to make a profit, not to match our most optimistic competitor. We never left customers – but they left us.

principles.text: Prefer simple propositions: many independent variables each likely to work still make success unlikely.
principles.quote: But if ten independent variables need to break favorably for a successful result, and each has a 90% probability of success, the likelihood of having a winner is only 35%.

principles.text: View stocks as fractional ownership of businesses, not tickers to trade on charts, brokers' opinions or near-term earnings.
principles.quote: Charlie and I ignore such distractions and instead view our holdings as fractional ownerships in businesses.

principles.text: Directors dependent on board fees are the least independent; where your treasure is, your heart is.
principles.quote: In our view, based on our considerable boardroom experience, the least independent directors are likely to be those who receive an important fraction of their annual income from the fees they receive for board service
